# Maturity, Ecosystem, and Limitations

Dimension covering alpha status, partner integrations (announced vs shipped),
GitHub activity, NVIDIA strategic positioning, and known limitations.

## Alpha Status

OpenShell launched March 16, 2026 at GTC [14]. Discovery agents report it is
described as alpha software in "single-player mode" (one developer, one
environment), though this specific terminology was not found in the fetched
NVIDIA documentation pages. The Futurum analyst warns of risk that "OpenShell
stalls at developer preview quality" [20].

Development status on PyPI listed as "3 - Alpha" with Python >= 3.12 required
(from discovery agent, unverified from primary sources).

## Version History

Discovery agents report version progression from v0.0.11 (March 19) to v0.0.16
within days of launch, suggesting rapid iteration. Specific version numbers

### Cisco DefenseClaw (Shipped)

Five scanning tools [16]:
1. **skill-scanner** — OpenClaw skill vulnerability analysis
2. **mcp-scanner** — Model Context Protocol server examination
3. **a2a-scanner** — Agent-to-agent security scanning
4. **CodeGuard** — Static analysis for AI-generated code
5. **AI Bill-of-Materials** — Documents AI stack dependencies

"Revoke sandbox permissions and remove network access within two seconds" [16].
Built-in observability "streaming to Splunk automatically" [16]. Deployment
claimed "under five minutes" [16].

### CrowdStrike Blueprint (Announced)

Four capability areas [15]:
1. AI Policy Enforcement (Falcon AIDR + OpenShell runtime)
2. Endpoint Protection (Falcon on DGX Spark/Station)
3. Cloud Runtime Protection (Falcon Cloud Security)
4. Identity Governance (Falcon Next-Gen Identity)

CBO Daniel Bernard: "Anything we could think about from a blast radius before
is unbounded. The human attacker needs to sleep a couple of hours a day. In the
agentic world, there's no such thing as a workday. It's work-always" [27].

### Trend Micro TrendAI (Announced)

Five-layer architecture [18]:
1. Centralized governance and compliance
2. Dynamic behavioral analysis (runtime observation)
3. Inline policy enforcement
4. AI application security (prompt/response inspection)
5. Continuous monitoring via agentic SIEM

## NVIDIA Strategic Positioning

Jensen Huang: "Employees will be supercharged by teams of frontier, specialized
and custom-built agents they deploy and manage" [14].

Futurum analyst: "NVIDIA wraps competitor models, controlling governance
boundaries regardless of model provider adoption — structural market advantage
masked by open licensing" [20]. Apache 2.0 license "removes adoption friction,
enables ecosystem standardization without vendor dependency" [20].

## Known Limitations

From Penligent [13]:
- "One trusted operator boundary per gateway" — not multi-tenant [13]
- Prompt injection: blast radius reduced, not prevented [13]
- Over 2,200 malicious skills on GitHub (Trend Micro data) [13]
- Agents inherit "broad credentials" — identity sprawl [13]
- Persistent state in ~/.openclaw survives sessions [13]
- "Operators repeatedly expose gateways on 0.0.0.0 without authentication" [13]
- "NemoClaw can make OpenClaw safer. It cannot make unsafe deployments safe by
  itself" [13]

From Futurum [20]:
- "Missing: third-party security audits, regulated-industry reference deployments"
- "Agent security, transparency, and accountability do not begin at the runtime
  layer" — OpenShell covers deployment only, not full lifecycle [20]
- "Sandbox implementation untested under real-world adversarial conditions" [20]

From VentureBeat [27] (source returned 429; data from search snippets —
individual statistics could not be verified against the full article):
- "The governance framework represents real progress. It also has three holes
  that every security leader deploying agentic AI will eventually hit"
- 48% of cybersecurity professionals rank agentic AI as top attack vector [27]
- Only 29% of organizations feel ready to deploy securely [27]

## Threat Landscape Context
